title: Mandy Gets It
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Dave Stuart Jr. shares a letter from a reader named Mandy, a Brooklyn high school English teacher who survived a challenging year of transition by grounding herself in his Five Key Beliefs methodology (Credibility, Effort, Efficacy, Belonging, Value). Mandy's letter is a practitioner's testimony to how a philosophical framework—not just a set of tactics—can provide stability when teaching conditions are destabilizing. Her most pressing challenge was students stuck in the lower levels of motivation (the 'red and orange sections of the Rainbow of Why'): students who had concluded that school had nothing to offer them in the world they were growing into. She connected this directly to AI: students using AI for everything because the rules seem no longer relevant and nobody agrees on new ones. Her response was a series of 'mini-sermons' about why school matters—how reading, writing, and discussion teach students to notice, to think clearly, to resist manipulation, to understand others. She describes designing an opening unit around 'School: why bother?' built on Everest statements and motivational readings. Stuart frames her letter as a model for 'inhabiting the role of teacher' rather than deploying a toolset—the deeper purpose of the Five Key Beliefs work.
points: A philosophical framework matters more than a tactical toolset in hard teaching years: Mandy credits the Five Key Beliefs with giving her the philosophical foundation she needed to reach students during a year when tactics alone would have been insufficient.

The AI motivation crisis is real and requires a direct pedagogical response: students using AI for everything are not primarily lazy—they have concluded that the rules are no longer relevant and nobody has given them new ones, which is a Value problem more than an integrity problem.

Mini-sermons about why school matters are a legitimate and underused pedagogical tool: helping students construct an answer to 'why should I bother' is not just motivational housekeeping—it is the precondition for any other learning to take hold.

Opening-unit design can directly address student motivation: Mandy plans a first-week unit around 'School: why bother?' using collaborative Everest statements, motivational readings, and student-written rationales, creating a foundation that the rest of the year builds on.

The Five Key Beliefs work is a way of inhabiting the role of teacher, not a collection of techniques: the difference between teachers who use it as a toolset and those who internalize it as a philosophy determines whether it sustains them through difficulty or just adds to their workload.
quotes: The most difficult part of the year for me was seeing really smart kids who had decided that there was no point in their bothering with school. They didn't see why they should pay attention, or do the reading, or come to class on time.

A lot of students are using AI for everything because they are getting a sense that the rules are no longer relevant, and nobody seems to agree on what the new rules should be. They just aren't really sure why anything they're learning in school will matter.

I gave a lot of mini-sermons throughout the year about why I think school, or at least English, matters — how reading, writing and discussing can teach us to pay attention to things we might otherwise not notice, and how noticing can make life richer; how school can help us to think more clearly and keep from being taken advantage of.
What we have the opportunity to do in school is so much bigger than just preparing to participate in the economy. We're preparing to participate in the world!

My goal is for students to spend time reading, thinking, talking, and writing about the question, 'School: why bother?' My goal is to collaboratively construct an Everest statement as a whole class that can be posted in the classroom, and for students to independently construct their own Everest statements for the year.
While I share lots of tips and tactics on this blog, what I've always been trying to describe isn't just a toolset, it's a way of being, a way of inhabiting the role of teacher.
